transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Thank you so much for seeing me, I really appreciate it. 

Um, well, I hope I'm explaining this right, but I came in because... well, I just always feel like I got a motor running inside me all day. It's not that I'm trying to be difficult or anything, I promise! It's just, if I have to sit still—like at church, or out there in the clinic waiting room, or even just at home—I start feeling real trapped. I just have to get up and do something, you know? 

Does that make sense? I hope that's okay to bring up.
Have you started or changed the dose of any medication—especially something like an antipsychotic, antidepressant, or anti-nausea drug—around the time this restless feeling began?

Oh, um, no sir. I haven't... I haven't started taking any new pills or anything like that. Not any of those, uh, depression ones or the stomach ones you mentioned. I don't really take much of anything, to be honest with you. 

Is that... is that okay? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions right. I hope I'm being helpful.

When you feel this need to keep moving, do you also notice a lot of worry or racing anxious thoughts going through your mind at the same time, or is it mainly just a physical feeling of restlessness without much worrying?

Well, um... no, I wouldn't say I'm worrying. I mean, I don't feel like I'm having bad thoughts or stressing out about things, I promise. It's really just... my body just wants to go. It's like my legs just won't listen to me when I tell them to stay put. 

I'm not a nervous person, really. I just... I just have a lot of energy, I guess. Is that what you meant? I hope I'm not making it sound worse than it is.
Have you noticed any unexplained weight loss, feeling unusually hot or sweaty, a racing heart, or shakiness in your hands along with this restless feeling?

Oh, no, sir. No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I eat just fine, I promise, and I haven't lost any weight. And my heart feels okay, I think. I don't get all sweaty or shaky or anything... well, unless it's just really hot outside, you know? But no, nothing strange like you're asking about. 

I hope that's a good thing? I really want to make sure I'm giving you the right answers. I don't want to waste your time or anything.
Thinking back, did you have this same kind of restlessness or trouble sitting still when you were a kid in school, or is this something that's only started more recently as an adult?

Um, well... yes, sir. I guess it's always been like this. Even back when I was a boy in school. 

I feel a little bad admitting it, because I really didn't want to be a bother to anyone, but... my teachers were always having to move my seat around. I just couldn't stay put, no matter how hard I tried. And I'd, um, I'd accidentally talk out of turn sometimes, or I'd get in a little trouble for jumping up out of my chair before class was even done. 

I promise I wasn't trying to be a bad kid or disrespectful! I just... my body was just like it is now, always needing to move. Does that make sense? I hope that's the kind of answer you needed. I just want to make sure I'm doing a good job explaining things for you.
Do you also have trouble staying focused on tasks—like losing track of what you're doing, forgetting things, or your mind wandering—separate from the physical restlessness?

Um, well, sir... I try real hard to pay attention, I promise I do. But, um... yeah, sometimes I guess my mind does wander a little bit. 

Like, when folks are talking to me about, you know, ride times, or going over pantry lists, or making plans for church... I always start out listening real good. I really do. But then... it's like my mind just slips off somewhere else without me meaning for it to, and I end up missing pieces I really needed to hear. 

I always feel awful about it, 'cause I don't want anyone thinking I'm ignoring them or that I don't care. I hope that doesn't make me sound lazy or rude? I really am trying my best to stay focused for people, sir. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about?

Would you say these problems with restlessness and losing focus have caused real difficulties for you—like trouble at work, in relationships, or in your daily responsibilities—in more than one area of your life?

Um, well, sir... I really hate to admit it, because I do try so hard to be helpful, but... yes, sir, I guess it has caused some trouble. 

I don't want you to think I'm undependable or anything, but... well, folks at church and at the pantry, and even my own family... they've sort of stopped trusting me with things. Like giving people rides, or keeping track of appointments, or organizing the supplies. I always mean to do a good job, I promise! But I just end up messing it up or losing track of things, and... and I feel like I just keep letting everybody down, even when my heart is in the right place. 

I'm really sorry if that makes me sound like a burden to folks. I don't want to be. Do you... do you think there's a way I can do better so they can trust me again? I just want to do right by everybody.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports lifelong (since childhood) motor restlessness ('motor running inside me'), inability to sit still in multiple settings (school, church, waiting rooms), impulsive behaviors as a child (talking out of turn, jumping out of seat), and current inattention symptoms (mind wandering during conversations, losing track of tasks, forgetting appointments). These symptoms have caused functional impairment across multiple domains—work/volunteer responsibilities (pantry, ride scheduling), family trust, and community roles (church). Medication-induced akathisia was ruled out (no new psychotropic or antiemetic medications), generalized anxiety was ruled out (no subjective worry or racing thoughts accompanying restlessness), and hyperthyroidism was ruled out (no weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia, or tremor). The combination of childhood-onset hyperactivity-impulsivity and inattention symptoms persisting into adulthood with cross-situational impairment supports a diagnosis of ADHD, combined presentation (F90.0), rather than a primary anxiety or medical/medication-induced condition.
